concept: Replication oplog window monitoring (Oplog GB/Hour, Replication Headroom)

claims.text: When lag exhausts retained oplog history, a secondary can no longer catch up from that history and may require a full resync. Monitor headroom and window together to detect the approach to that boundary. (high confidence)

Atlas documentation states that replication headroom is collected at 85-second intervals regardless of project default granularity. Treat this as a sampled diagnostic signal when interpreting short workload bursts. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Ops Manager's troubleshooting documentation lists idle or infrequent writes as a possible cause of misleading reported lag and recommends checking whether lag persists; this is a documented diagnostic caveat, not evidence that every modern Atlas lag spike has that cause. (low confidence)

Replication headroom is the relevant sync source oplog window minus the secondary’s replication lag; it measures remaining history margin rather than free disk space. Atlas alert documentation names the sync source, while its metric overview describes the primary. (high confidence)

An oplog window is workload-sensitive: rising oplog generation can shrink the window. Operational inference: compare window and lag trends after workload or capacity changes rather than treating a previous window measurement as a future guarantee. (medium confidence)

The oplog window describes retained operation time. Percona measures the newest-to-oldest entry span in seconds; Atlas presents an estimated average in hours based on oplog churn. Normalize units before comparing either window with lag. (high confidence)
Oplog GB/Hour measures the primary's average hourly generation of oplog data; a high generation rate relative to configured oplog size corresponds to a short recovery window. (high confidence)

Operational inference for storage auto-scaling: monitor storage separately from replication headroom. Atlas documents that insufficient oplog size can prevent disk auto-scaling; rising disk capacity therefore does not, by itself, establish adequate retained replication history. (medium confidence)

Grafana’s MongoDB integration documents separate critical alerts for excessive replication lag and low replication headroom. The public monitoring-mixins alert implementation also separates these two conditions. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

The inspected monitoring-mixins headroom rule averages oplog spans and member optimes by job and mongodb_cluster, and fires at a non-positive result for five minutes. Inference: these averages can conceal one badly lagging secondary, so assess member-level headroom as well as aggregate alerts. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
Atlas describes Oplog GB/Hour in terms of uncompressed oplog data. Treating this number as compressed physical disk growth would conflate different measurements. (low confidence)
Atlas defines Replication Headroom as the primary's replication oplog window minus the secondary's replication lag. (low confidence)
Monitor headroom alongside replication lag to assess whether a secondary risks falling outside retained oplog history; lag alone does not describe the remaining history margin. (high confidence)

Percona's ReplSet Summary defines its recovery window as newest-entry timestamp minus oldest-entry timestamp. Its Oplog Details dashboard separately labels Oplog Range and Now to End, with the latter measured from the current time to the oldest entry; these panel definitions should not be assumed interchangeable with Atlas's churn-based estimate. (medium confidence)

Percona's Oplog Details buffer-capacity panel measures fetched but unapplied entries, with Used and Max in bytes. That buffer is distinct from the time span of retained oplog history. (low confidence)
Grafana Cloud's documented MongoDB integration includes a ReplicaSet dashboard and a MongodbReplicationHeadroom condition for low headroom. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
